rationale: Start with a broad scouting gradient to capture all 10 compounds while retaining early peaks. Their elution window and weakest resolutions will guide window trimming, gradient slope, and temperature optimization.
Lengthen only the gradient to test whether the limiting pair responds to a shallower slope. The last peak should remain below 10 minutes, leaving room to improve resolution without a time penalty.

Narrowing the gradient makes its slope approximately equivalent to a 16-minute scouting gradient, which should bring the limiting pair near full resolution. Raising the starting organic fraction should offset the added retention and keep the last peak below 10 minutes.

Further narrow the gradient to raise the limiting pair above R = 1.5, following its improvement with decreasing slope. The higher starting organic fraction should keep the last peak below 10 minutes while preserving ample separation of the early peaks.
Injection 4 already achieves the maximum CRF, so retain it as the benchmark. Test a 5 °C temperature increase to shorten elution while checking whether the limiting pair maintains R ≥ 1.5.

Return to 40 °C, where full resolution was achieved, and raise phi0 to shorten retention. The slightly shallower gradient should help preserve the limiting pair’s resolution while testing a faster alternative to injection 4.

Reduce the gradient slope slightly from injection 6 to recover the limiting pair’s resolution while retaining its higher starting organic fraction. This should keep the last peak below 10 minutes and may provide another maximum-score method.

The maximum CRF is already secured; test a substantially faster method using a shorter gradient and higher temperature. Moving beyond the near-coelution at 45 °C may separate that pair again after an elution-order reversal, but all adjacent pairs must be checked.

Lower temperature by 5 °C to move the new limiting pair away from its near-coelution at 60 °C. This isolates temperature selectivity while preserving the shorter gradient and ample margin below the 10-minute threshold.

Lengthen the gradient at 55 °C to test whether the limiting pair gains enough resolution for a faster maximum-score method. Monitor the other close pair as well, since its temperature-induced order reversal may make it respond differently to slope.

Slightly reduce the gradient slope to lift the limiting pair above R = 1.5, based on its improvement between injections 9 and 10. The last peak should remain below 10 minutes, potentially achieving maximum CRF faster than the established 40 °C methods.

Test a faster high-temperature branch by shortening the gradient from injection 8. The limiting pair appears to reverse order between 55 and 60 °C, so a steeper gradient may increase its separation rather than compress it.

Shift injection 9’s gradient window downward while keeping its slope unchanged to test starting-composition selectivity for the limiting pair. This may recover full resolution with earlier final elution than injection 11, while improving retention of the earliest peaks.

Shorten injection 13’s gradient to seek a faster maximum-score method. The previously limiting pair now has resolution margin, and the current closest pair may benefit slightly from the steeper slope, based on the earlier 55 °C runs.

Slightly flatten injection 14’s gradient to raise its limiting resolution from 1.32 to approximately 1.5 while preserving the other close pair. This should elute the last peak around 7.8 minutes, faster than the current fully resolved methods.

Injection 15 secures maximum CRF with final elution at 7.76 minutes; explore a cooler, steeper-gradient branch for further shortening. Lower temperature may separate the central cluster differently, so this run will check for useful order reversals and new limiting pairs.

Return to the successful 55 °C branch and lower the starting organic fraction to improve selectivity of the limiting pair. Pair this with a steeper, shorter gradient to test whether full resolution can be retained with earlier final elution than injection 15.

Retain injection 17 as the fastest fully resolved method and test a higher-starting-organic, high-temperature alternative. Relative to injection 12, shifting the window upward at unchanged slope may improve the central limiting pair, though early-peak resolution is a risk.

Test a slightly steeper slope than injection 17 to locate the speed limit of the fastest fully resolved branch. The last peak should elute sooner, but the central pair with R = 1.59 may fall below baseline resolution; injection 17 remains the benchmark.

Explore an untested intermediate-temperature, steep-gradient branch for a faster fully resolved separation. The central cluster has shown order reversals with temperature and slope, so this is a selectivity test rather than an assumed improvement over injection 17.

Test a slightly shallower slope than injection 15 to improve its weakest pair while preserving the other close separation. This targets a better-balanced maximum-score method, with final elution still comfortably below 10 minutes.

Slightly flatten injection 11’s gradient to increase its limiting pair’s resolution while retaining separation of the other close pair. This targets more resolution margin at maximum CRF, with the last peak expected just below 10 minutes.

Test a slope between injections 11 and 22 to balance the two closest pairs near R = 1.7. This should preserve maximum CRF with slightly earlier final elution than injection 22 and more resolution margin than the fastest methods.

Trim the endpoint to just beyond the observed elution window while using a slope between injections 11 and 23. This should retain full resolution with balanced margins, elute the last peak around 9.2 minutes, and shorten the programmed gradient to 10 minutes.

Trim injection 21’s gradient endpoint while preserving its starting composition, temperature, and slope. All peaks should elute before the gradient ends at the outlet, retaining its maximum CRF and approximately 8-minute final elution with a shorter programmed gradient.
